summary: Announces a questionnaire sent to every host on the early ARPANET. The answers about each machine's terminals and operation were meant to help the people designing a full Telnet specification. A small committee would phone each site to record answers and publish the results as an RFC; RFC 112 later summarized them.

eli5.summary: Before building a toy that works with every kind of TV, you first ask each family what TV they own. This note is that list of questions, sent to every computer site.

subtitle: A 1971 questionnaire asking every ARPANET host how its terminals and character handling work, to inform Telnet.

tldr.problem: Implementers of early Telnet versions and the User/Server Site Protocol Committee needed to know how different Network hosts handle terminals and operate.
tldr.mechanism: A four-person committee circulates a 10-question questionnaire to each host's Technical Liaison and phones every site to record the answers.
tldr.outcome: The results were to be tabulated and distributed as an RFC. This RFC only contains the questions.

today: The metadata gives this RFC an Unknown status and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a historical survey form from the early Network, and only the blank questionnaire is printed in it.

sections.title: Why the Survey
sections.content:
RFC 106 is dated 3 March 1971 and was written by Thomas O'Sullivan of RDS. It says that answers about the characteristics and operation of Network HOSTs will help implementers of some early versions of TELNET and the User/Server Site Protocol Committee as it considers a full TELNET specification.

The Technical Liaison contact at each HOST site is asked to review the questions. A committee member will phone each site within a few days to record the answers. The committee is Bob Long (SDC), John Melvin (SRI/ARC), Ed Meyer (MIT/MAC) and Tom O'Sullivan (RDS).
sections.eli5: A few people building a way for far-away terminals to talk to other computers first want to learn how each computer treats keyboards. So they phone every site with questions.

sections.title: What the Questionnaire Asks
sections.content:
The form has ten numbered questions, with a separate form for each HOST directly interfaced to an IMP. It asks, for example, whether the system works on input one character at a time or one line at a time, and what maximum buffer size it gives for input and output of a physical line.

Other questions cover the effect of the CR, LF, NL and CR,LF keystrokes, the special characters used to awaken a process during data entry (such as control C or break), the keyboard terminal types and codes supported, and the internal character code (if not ASCII or EBCDIC, a copy of the code is to be attached).

The rest ask which duplex modes each terminal type supports, whether an optional-echo terminal is assumed to need echo at connect time, whether the system detects errors such as parity on terminal input, and what end-of-line sequence is used for punched paper tape.
sections.eli5: The questions are things like: do you read one letter at a time or a whole line, and what happens when someone presses Return?

sections.title: What Happens to the Answers
sections.content: The RFC says results of the questionnaire will be tabulated and distributed as an RFC. The text printed here is the blank form, so it carries no answers itself.
sections.eli5: This note only has the empty questions. The filled-in answers were to be shared later.
